blocks.content: Kashmir's ancient history is unusually well-documented for early India because of Kalhana's 12th-century chronicle Rajatarangini, which is frequently cited in exams as one of India's earliest works of systematic historical writing. This chapter traces Kashmir from its early legendary origins through its major ancient dynasties.

blocks.title: Key Takeaways
items: According to Nilamata Purana, Kashmir was originally a lake known as Sati Saras, drained by Sage Kashyapa.
Emperor Ashoka introduced Buddhism to Kashmir and established the city of Srinagari.
The 4th Buddhist Council was hosted at Kundalvana under Kushan Emperor Kanishka.
Kalhana authored Rajatarangini in Sanskrit, considered one of the earliest authentic historical chronicles of India.
Lalitaditya Muktapida of the Karkota Dynasty constructed the iconic Martand Sun Temple and expanded the kingdom.

blocks.content: Kashmiri tradition, recorded in the Nilamata Purana and later in Kalhana's Rajatarangini, holds that the Kashmir Valley was once a vast lake called 'Satisar', drained by the sage Kashyapa (from whom the name 'Kashmir' is popularly derived as 'Kashyapa-mira' or 'the lake of Kashyapa'), making the region habitable.
Kashmir finds mention in early Sanskrit literature and appears to have been part of the wider cultural and political sphere of ancient India from at least the Mauryan period onward.
Kashmir may be conquered by the force of spiritual merit, but not by the force of arms.

items: Kashmir is traditionally associated with Emperor Ashoka of the Mauryan dynasty (3rd century BCE), who is credited in later tradition with founding the city of Srinagari (an early precursor associated with, though not identical in location to, present-day Srinagar) and with introducing Buddhism to the Valley.

Under the Kushan Empire (1st-3rd centuries CE), Kashmir became a significant centre of Buddhist learning and practice; King Kanishka is traditionally associated with convening the Fourth Buddhist Council, which — according to widely cited tradition — was held in Kashmir (at Kundalvana, near modern Srinagar, according to some accounts), marking a high point of Buddhist scholarship in the region.

This Buddhist heritage left a lasting imprint on Kashmir's art, architecture and learning traditions, visible today in archaeological sites such as Harwan (near Srinagar) with its distinctive terracotta tile work.

blocks.content: ★ EXAM POINT: The Fourth Buddhist Council's traditional association with Kashmir (under Kanishka) is a frequently tested ancient-history fact — remember Kashmir's early Buddhist centre-of-learning status, distinct from its later, better-known Hindu-Shaivite and then Islamic religious history.

blocks.content: The Karkota dynasty (approximately 7th-9th centuries CE) is considered one of ancient Kashmir's most powerful ruling houses, with King Lalitaditya Muktapida (8th century) traditionally credited with an extensive military expansion and major architectural patronage, including the celebrated Martand Sun Temple near Anantnag — one of the most significant ancient temple complexes of the Valley, now preserved as a protected archaeological monument in ruins.

Kalhana's Rajatarangini ('River of Kings'), composed in Sanskrit around 1148-50 CE, is celebrated as one of the earliest systematic historical chronicles produced anywhere in ancient/medieval India, covering Kashmir's dynastic history from legendary antiquity down to Kalhana's own time under the Lohara dynasty, and remains a primary source for reconstructing early Kashmiri history.

The Utpala dynasty (9th-10th centuries CE), including rulers such as Avantivarman (who commissioned significant irrigation works improving the Valley's agricultural productivity) and the later Lohara dynasty, continued this tradition of temple-building and administrative development through to the eve of the region's transition toward Islamic rule from the 14th century onward.

items: Kalhana wrote Rajatarangini in Sanskrit during the reign of King Jayasimha of the Lohara dynasty.
The 4th Buddhist Council at Kundalvana (presided by Vasumitra) led to the formal division into Hinayana and Mahayana.
Lalitaditya Muktapida of the Karkota dynasty is frequently tested for building the Martand Sun Temple and his military conquests.

blocks.content: ★ EXAM POINT: Martand Sun Temple (near Anantnag, built under Lalitaditya Muktapida of the Karkota dynasty) is Kashmir's most significant ancient Hindu temple ruin — a frequently tested monument-cum-dynasty pairing.

items: Kashmir traditionally derived from 'Kashyapa-mira'; legend holds the Valley was once the lake 'Satisar', drained by sage Kashyapa.
Kanishka (Kushan Empire) traditionally associated with the Fourth Buddhist Council, held in Kashmir.
Karkota dynasty's Lalitaditya Muktapida (8th century) built the Martand Sun Temple; a major territorial expander.
Kalhana's Rajatarangini (composed ~1148-50 CE) = one of ancient/medieval India's earliest systematic historical chronicles, covering Kashmir's dynastic history.
Avantivarman (Utpala dynasty) is noted for major irrigation works benefiting Valley agriculture.
